title: The setting sun
hook: the first visualization: the setting sun, like a drum hung in the west

segments.voice: Yesterday, Queen Vaidehi in her locked room, asking the Buddha for a land without sorrow, and then asking how to see it. Your line was a land without sorrow. Who did you listen to a little longer? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-one.

How do I see it? That was the queen's question, and it's a hard one. The land of bliss lies in the west, and nobody can walk there or look there. So the Buddha's first answer is almost startling in how plain it is. No chant. No doctrine. No secret. He tells her to look at something anyone can see on a clear evening. The sun, going down in the west. Today: the setting sun.
screen: `HOW DO I SEE IT?` → `NO CHANT, NO SECRET.` → `THE SETTING SUN.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. In the meditation sutra, the Buddha tells Vaidehi to sit facing west, and to look at the sun as it is about to set. Fix the mind on it, he says, steadily, without letting the thought wander anywhere else. Second, the image. As the sun sinks, the sutra says, it looks like a drum hanging in the sky. Round, full, still, hung in the west. Then comes the real work: hold that image. Keep it clear, the sutra says, whether the eyes are open or closed. The sunset ends. The drum stays. The sutra calls this the first meditation, the perception of the sun. Third, why the sun. The land of bliss lies in the west, and every evening the setting sun points that way. So the first step toward a land no one can see starts from the one thing anyone can see. In Japanese this practice is called nissokan, the sun contemplation. Fourth, where it leads. The sun is only the first rung of a ladder. The meditations that follow climb, one image at a time, from things the eyes know toward the land itself, and toward Amitabha. Each image steadies the mind enough to hold the next. Tomorrow's rung is water. For today, the whole practice fits in one evening: a person, a window facing west, and a sun hung like a drum, held in the mind after the light is gone.
screen: `SIT FACING WEST.` · `A DRUM HANGING IN THE SKY.` · `THE ONE THING ANYONE CAN SEE.` · `THE FIRST RUNG OF A LADDER.` · then, large: `THE DRUM IN THE WEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. If the sun is setting where you are, turn toward it, without staring straight into it. If it isn't, close your eyes and call up a sunset you remember. Let the sun hang low and round in the west, like a drum. Hold it there. When the image fades or the mind drifts, gently bring the drum back. Nothing to add, nothing to figure out. Just the sun, held steady. The bell holds the time.
The setting sun. The first meditation given to Queen Vaidehi: sit facing west, look at the sinking sun like a drum hung in the sky, and hold the image with eyes open or closed. Today's word.
Your line: the drum in the west. This evening, find out which way west is from where you live, and if you can, watch the sun go down there. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Following the meditation sutra, some Pure Land practitioners sit facing west at sunset and hold the image of the setting sun in mind; in Japanese this is called nissokan, the sun contemplation.

notes: First meditation paraphrased from the Amitayur-dhyana Sutra (Takakusu 1894 is not on the validator's public-domain list, so nothing is quoted). Confirm: sit facing west, the sun about to set, 'like a drum suspended', eyes open or closed, 'the first meditation'.
The total number of meditations is left out deliberately; the script says only that the meditations climb one image at a time.
Nissokan (日想観) as the Japanese name of the sun contemplation: confirm reading and characters.
Practice cautions against staring into the sun.

Editor: 'past a great many Buddha-worlds' removed (that distance is from the short sutra; the meditation sutra cited today has the Buddha say Amitabha is not far away). Cut the invented detail that Vaidehi watched the sunset every evening from a palace roof or prison window, the 'red' sun, and 'everyone can see'.
